title: The direct path
hook: a direct path for the purification of beings: four foundations of mindfulness (MN 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: your immeasurables, all four rooms in one sitting. Your line was immeasurable. Did you visit each room once? Day two hundred forty-six, and a new part of the path.

The word mindfulness is everywhere now. It's on apps, in office trainings, on the side of a tea box. Most of it traces back, one way or another, to a single old text: a talk the Buddha is said to have given to the people of Kuru, in a market town called Kammasadhamma. For the next three weeks, we'll walk through it, section by section. It's long, it repeats itself on purpose, and it's one of the most practiced texts in the Buddhist world. Today: the opening line, and the map. Today's word: satipatthana.
screen: `MINDFULNESS, ON A TEA BOX.` → `ONE OLD TEXT.` → `THREE WEEKS, SECTION BY SECTION.`

segments.voice: The text is the Satipatthana Sutta, number ten in the Middle Length Discourses, with a longer twin, the Maha-satipatthana, in the Long Discourses. Sati means mindfulness, remembering to be present. Patthana is usually taken as foundation or establishing, though scholars argue about how to split the word. So: the establishing of mindfulness. It opens with a bold claim. The Buddha says this is the ekayana path, for the purification of beings, for getting past sorrow and grief, for the ending of pain and distress, for finding the true way, for realizing nibbana. Ekayana is a puzzle. Older English translations said the only way. Many modern ones say the direct path, or the one-way path, a road that goes straight to one place. The word itself can bear several meanings, and teachers disagree. Then comes the map. There are four foundations, four places to set mindfulness down. The body. Feelings, meaning the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of experience. The mind, its states and moods. And dhammas, a hard word here, often translated mental qualities or phenomena: the patterns the Buddha taught people to recognize. One path, four doors into it. Every section of the sutta that follows fits somewhere on this map. For the next three weeks, when you get lost, come back to these four. Body, feelings, mind, dhammas.
screen: `SATI + PATTHANA: ESTABLISHING MINDFULNESS.` · `EKAYANA: ONLY, OR DIRECT?` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `ONE PATH, FOUR DOORS.` · then, large: `ONE WAY, FOUR DOORS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. We'll touch each door once. Body: feel where you're sitting, the weight, the contact. Feelings: is this moment pleasant, unpleasant, or neither? Mind: what's the mood right now, calm, restless, tired? Dhammas: is anything pulling at you, a want, an irritation, a doubt? Name the four quietly to yourself: body, feelings, mind, dhammas. Then just sit and let the breath be. The bell holds the time.
Satipatthana. The establishing of mindfulness, set down in four places: body, feelings, mind and dhammas.
Your line: one way, four doors. Today, try to say the four foundations from memory three times: body, feelings, mind, dhammas. Day two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: The Satipatthana Sutta is studied and practiced across the Buddhist world, especially in Theravada communities, where many meditation methods, including the Burmese insight traditions, trace themselves to it; the longer version is often chanted in full.

original.note: Pali satipaṭṭhāna: the establishing, or foundation, of mindfulness.

trapdoor: what you thought: satipatthana is just a long word for mindfulness.
what it means: mindfulness set down in four places: body, feelings, mind, dhammas.
what a scholar hears: the compound can split as sati + paṭṭhāna (foundation) or sati + upaṭṭhāna (establishing, being present); commentators and modern scholars read it both ways.
